hook: Hundreds of MCP servers exist — filesystem, GitHub, databases. Using them well is a **security and governance exercise** wearing a configuration file.

scenes.title: Reference servers: don't build what already exists
scenes.sub: The maintained menagerie and what each is for
scenes.narration: Before writing a line of MCP code, know the shelf. The reference implementations cover the everyday cases: filesystem — read, write, and search files under an allowed directory, with the path-scoping guardrails from AG-03 built in; database servers — Postgres, SQLite, running SQL against configured connections with read-only modes; GitHub — issues, pull requests, repository search, letting agents work your repos through curated tools; fetch — retrieving web content for the agent; plus memory, Slack, Google Drive and hundreds of community servers. The point isn't a catalog — it's the strategy: these are MAINTAINED by the community, follow spec updates like AG-05's stateless core, and have been reviewed by more eyes than anything you'll write quickly. Consume first; build only what's missing.

items.s: Scoped to allowed directories · the AG-03 workspace pattern, standardized
Configured connections · read-only modes · GA-18's fences at the server boundary
Issues, PRs, code search · agents that triage, summarize and draft — your token, your repos

scenes.narration: Two usage patterns cover most adoption. Local stdio servers — filesystem, memory — configure in your host's settings file, run as local processes, perfect for personal productivity agents. Remote servers — a team's internal tools, SaaS connectors — run over HTTP with real auth, which is where AG-07's security practices become mandatory. A concrete composed example: an IDE agent with filesystem plus GitHub plus a database server can answer 'which issues mention the payment module and what do the logs say' — three servers, one conversation, zero custom integration code. That's the N-times-M collapse paying rent. The discipline: start from the reference implementation even when building custom — fork, scope down, keep the security defaults.

scenes.title: Configuration is a security surface
scenes.sub: How hosts load servers — and what each line grants
scenes.narration: Connecting a stdio server means an entry in the host's config: a command, arguments, environment variables. Understand what you're declaring: the command runs with YOUR user permissions — a server entry is executable code installation, as surely as pip-installing a package; environment variables are secrets in plaintext config — API keys in a config file deserve the same care as .env files; arguments like allowed-directories ARE the security policy for filesystem-type servers — the difference between 'read my project' and 'read my entire home directory including SSH keys'. Remote servers add a URL and an auth flow — and OAuth consent screens are the user's one chance to see what they're granting. Treat config edits as code changes: reviewed, versioned, minimal.

scenes.title: A host config, read as a policy document
annot: The filesystem path argument IS the sandbox — one directory, not your home folder
GITHUB_TOKEN: use a fine-grained token scoped to exactly the repos the agent needs
Remote server: the URL's operator can see every request — internal servers still need TLS + auth (AG-07)
scenes.narration: Read the config as capabilities, not convenience. The filesystem server's path argument is its entire security model — keep it at project scope; the moment it points at your home directory, every prompt-injection in any document the agent reads can reach your SSH keys. The GitHub token deserves fine-grained scoping — a classic full-access PAT in a config file turns a clever prompt into repo-wide damage. The remote entry raises the operator question: who runs mcp-dot-corp, what do they log, is the transport authenticated and encrypted — enterprise answers come next reel via gateways. Rule of thumb: if you wouldn't paste a line into a shell, don't paste it into this config without thinking.

scenes.title: An MCP server is a supply-chain dependency. **Audit it like one.**
scenes.narration: The uncomfortable math: an MCP server holds credentials and executes actions — a malicious or compromised server is a malicious or compromised employee. So evaluate servers like dependencies. Provenance: prefer official or reference implementations from the ecosystem's known maintainers over random registry entries; a server from the vendor whose API it wraps beats a third party re-implementation. Behavior review: read what it exposes — the tool list is the attack surface; a 'filesystem' server that also shells out to curl is not a filesystem server. Permissions: does it request the minimum scopes for its job — a read-only search server wanting write tokens is a red flag. Update posture: does it track spec revisions — AG-05's deprecations — or is it abandoned? And npx-running servers execute freshly fetched code — pin versions.

items.s: Official/reference implementations · vendor-authored for their own APIs · known maintainers
The tool list IS the attack surface · unexpected capabilities = investigate or decline
Version-pinned installs · track spec updates · abandoned servers are liabilities

scenes.narration: The pin-versions point deserves expansion because npx and pip-style invocations make it invisible: 'npx some-server' fetches and executes the LATEST package at run time — a supply-chain attack on the package becomes an attack on you, automatically. Pin the version, and let updates be a deliberate diff you review. For internal adoption, run a registry review process: a curated allow-list of approved servers, vetted once, versioned, with the vetting recorded — the same discipline as approving open-source libraries, which is exactly what these are. And log what servers are connected where: shadow IT MCP servers — a developer connecting a random calendar server — are the 2026 version of the unauthorized SaaS integration, with the same data-exfiltration shape.

scenes.title: MCP gateways: the enterprise control plane
scenes.sub: One front door for every server
scenes.narration: Individual config files don't scale to an enterprise — that's what MCP gateways solve. A gateway sits between hosts and servers: the organization's servers sit behind it; employees' hosts connect to the gateway, not to servers directly. What the gateway adds: centralized auth — one identity integration, SSO, per-user permissions instead of per-server token sprawl; audit — every tool call logged, attributable, reviewable — the compliance answer to 'what did the AI do?'; policy — which servers and tools each user or group may reach, enforced at the boundary; lifecycle — servers are registered, versioned, and swapped without touching thousands of host configs. The gateway turns a folder of JSON configs into infrastructure: operated, observed, governed.

layers.s: One gateway endpoint · no per-server credentials on endpoints
AuthN/AuthZ per user · full call audit · policy enforcement · server registry
Internal + vetted third-party · credentials live HERE, not on endpoints

scenes.narration: The security win in one picture: credentials move from thousands of endpoints into the gateway's vault; employees bring identity, not secrets; every call passes a policy check and lands in an audit log. This is the same pattern as API gateways before it — and it inherits the same operational truths: the gateway is now critical infrastructure — high availability, monitoring, careful rollout of policy changes; governance must stay fast enough not to be routed around — a gateway so slow to approve new servers that developers run local stdio servers in secret has failed its purpose. For a team of five, a gateway is overkill — configs and reviews suffice. For five hundred, it's how MCP stays a platform instead of becoming an incident generator.

scenes.title: Connected and governed. Now the threat model in detail.

recap: Consume before building: reference servers (filesystem, DB, GitHub) are maintained and spec-current — fork and scope, don't start from zero
Host configs are security policy: the filesystem path argument is the sandbox, tokens deserve fine-grained scopes, remote URLs need an operator you trust
Servers are supply-chain dependencies: provenance, pinned versions, audited tool surfaces; gateways centralize auth, audit, and policy at enterprise scale

quiz.q: Why is 'npx -y some-mcp-server' a supply-chain risk?
opts: It fetches and executes the LATEST package at runtime — a compromised release executes automatically
quiz.why: Unpinned package execution is arbitrary-code delivery from the package registry; pin versions and review updates deliberately.

quiz.q: What does an MCP gateway centralize for an enterprise?
opts: AuthN/AuthZ, audit logging, policy enforcement, and the server registry — with credentials off endpoints
quiz.why: One front door replaces per-endpoint credentials and configs with governed, auditable infrastructure.

quiz.q: A read-only search MCP server requests a write-scoped API token. What should you do?
opts: Treat it as a red flag: grant minimum scopes, or decline the server
Give it an admin token instead
quiz.why: Permission requests beyond function are a core trust signal — least privilege applies to servers exactly as to users.

code.title: The server-vetting checklist
code.body:
# Before adding ANY MCP server to your stack:

provenance:
  □ Official/reference impl, or vendor-authored for its own API?
  □ Known maintainers, public repo, issue responsiveness?

surface:
  □ Read the exposed tools — does each match the server's stated job?
  □ Any unexpected capabilities (shell, network, file writes)?

permissions:
  □ Minimum scopes? Read-only where possible?
  □ Credentials scoped to specific repos/paths, not broad?

operations:
  □ Version pinned (npx pkg@1.2.3 / lockfile), not latest?
  □ Tracks MCP spec revisions (post-2026-07-28 aware)?
  □ Logged in the team server registry (no shadow IT)?

# 2 minutes per server. Cheaper than one incident.
annot: The checklist is short on purpose — it has to be usable on every adoption decision
'Unexpected capabilities' is the highest-signal line: scope creep in a tool list is how benign servers become dangerous
Registry logging closes the loop: you can't audit what you don't know is connected

notes:
# Using Existing MCP Servers

## Reference servers
- Filesystem (scoped dirs) · databases (read-only modes) · GitHub · fetch · hundreds community-maintained.
- Strategy: consume → fork/scope → build only what's missing.

## Connecting
- stdio = local config: command + args + env. Config IS security policy.
- Filesystem path arg = the sandbox. Tokens fine-grained. Remote URLs need trusted operators.

## Trust (supply chain)
- Provenance (official/vendor) · read the tool surface · minimum scopes · pin versions · track spec updates · registry (no shadow IT).

## Gateways
- Enterprise control plane: central auth (SSO), full audit, policy, server registry.
- Credentials off endpoints. Critical infra — but governance must stay fast.
